passages.text: LEPROSY, a foul cutaneous disease, appearing in dry, white, thin, scurfy scabs, sometimes attended with great itching.

The leprosy of the Arabians, or elephantiasis, is far more dreadful: the skin grows thick and tuberculated, the face swells, the voice becomes hoarse, and the fingers and toes lose all feeling and at length drop off.
In the middle ages it was so common in Europe that there were lazar-houses for lepers in almost every town; but it has now nearly disappeared from these kingdoms.
It is thought to be hereditary, and to be caused by a gross diet of salt fish and putrid meat, and by want of cleanliness.
It was formerly held to be highly contagious, and lepers were therefore shut out from the society of other men.
When the disease is confirmed it is reckoned incurable.

Leprosy, also known as Hansen's disease, is a long-term infection by the bacteria Mycobacterium leprae or Mycobacterium lepromatosis. It mainly damages the nerves, the skin, the eyes and the lining of the nose.

Nerve damage leads to a loss of feeling in the hands and feet. Because injuries then go unnoticed, repeated wounds and infections can cause the loss of fingers and toes; the disease itself does not make body parts fall off.
In the lepromatous form, the skin thickens and forms nodules, especially on the face.
Gerhard Armauer Hansen identified the bacterium in 1873. It was the first bacterium found to cause disease in humans.

Leprosy spreads between people, probably through droplets from the nose and mouth, after months of close contact. It is not highly contagious: about 95% of people who are exposed do not develop the disease.
Leprosy is curable with multidrug therapy, a combination of antibiotics recommended by the World Health Organization since 1981 and given free of charge.
Leprosy was common in medieval Europe, where sufferers were often placed in leper colonies or leprosaria. It later declined in most of Europe. Patients still face stigma and isolation in many places.
Older texts used the word leprosy for many skin diseases, which were probably not Hansen's disease.

reasons: Rare terms appear in both: lepers, loss of feeling, fingers and toes, thickened skin.
Elephantiasis also scores, but today that word names a different disease, so it is listed as a candidate only.

alignments.label: What the word covers

wikipedia.quote: Older texts used the word leprosy for many skin diseases

alignments.note: A change in language. In 1810 'leprosy' also named scaly skin diseases; today it names only Hansen's disease.

alignments.label: Loss of feeling

britannica.quote: the fingers and toes lose all feeling

wikipedia.quote: Nerve damage leads to a loss of feeling in the hands and feet

alignments.note: Same sign. Wikipedia names the cause: nerve damage.

alignments.label: Fingers dropping off

wikipedia.quote: the disease itself does not make body parts fall off

alignments.note: Fingers and toes are lost, but through unnoticed injuries, not because the disease rots them away.

britannica.quote: the skin grows thick and tuberculated

wikipedia.quote: the skin thickens and forms nodules

britannica.quote: there were lazar-houses for lepers in almost every town

wikipedia.quote: sufferers were often placed in leper colonies or leprosaria

alignments.label: Diet as the cause

britannica.quote: caused by a gross diet of salt fish and putrid meat

wikipedia.quote: a long-term infection by the bacteria Mycobacterium leprae

alignments.note: Diet is replaced by a bacterium, found in 1873.

alignments.label: Hereditary

britannica.quote: It is thought to be hereditary

alignments.note: Inference: cases in families come from long close contact, not inheritance.

alignments.label: Highly contagious

britannica.quote: It was formerly held to be highly contagious

alignments.note: The 1810 entry already doubts the old view, and Wikipedia agrees. But the disease does pass between people.

alignments.label: Incurable

wikipedia.quote: Leprosy is curable with multidrug therapy

alignments.note: True in 1810, no longer: antibiotics cure it.

alignments.label: Hansen's bacterium

wikipedia.quote: It was the first bacterium found to cause disease in humans

alignments.note: A landmark for germ theory, 63 years after this edition.

suggestedQuestions: Is the 1810 leprosy the same disease as leprosy today?
Do fingers and toes really drop off with leprosy?
Was the 1810 entry right that leprosy is incurable?

Is the 1810 leprosy the same disease as.answer: Only in part. The 1810 entry uses the word for a scaly skin disease with dry white scabs [B1] and for a worse form with thick skin and loss of feeling [B2]. Wikipedia says older texts used the word for many skin diseases that were probably not Hansen's disease [W8]. The second form [B2] matches the modern description of nerve damage and thickened skin [W2] [W3].

Do fingers and toes really drop off with.answer: Not directly. The 1810 entry says the fingers and toes lose all feeling and at length drop off [B2]. Wikipedia says the loss of feeling is real, but fingers and toes are lost through repeated unnoticed injuries and infections; the disease itself does not make them fall off [W2].

Was the 1810 entry right that leprosy is.answer: It was right for 1810, but not today. The entry says the confirmed disease is reckoned incurable [B6]. Wikipedia says leprosy is curable with multidrug therapy, recommended by the World Health Organization since 1981 [W6].
